QotD: Soothsayer Carmichael knows everything he would need to know in order to perform magic, yet he can’t perform magic. Whatever the thing you use to perform magic is, let’s say for the sake of argument that it’s a specific portion of your soul…he just plain doesn’t have that portion. Would you be okay with saying that this qualifies him as a disabled person, and writing several stories in which he’s used as an analogy for being blind or deaf or mute, in the same way that X-Men stories are often analogies for racist or LGBT issues?

Hmm, interesting query, that. I’m inclined to say no, as I personally define a disability as something that prevents one from doing something that the average person frequently does; not something that prevents one from doing something exceptional and extraordinary.

Like, for example, I wouldn’t say that someone who can’t curl their tongue has a disability, or someone who for whatever reason can’t give blood transfusions, as those aren’t really typical activities. It’s kind of like not having photographic (or eidetic) memory; all it does is prevent you from doing the extraordinary, not the ordinary.

I suppose, however, that this does depend on the rarity in the population of the Sentinels Universe of that portion of the soul, that potential to do magic. (Which, for brevity’s sake, I’m just gonna call Magery, as that’s what a similar concept is called in the GURPS RPG.) If most folks do possess Magery, but just have never learned how to harness it (for obvious reasons), then I suppose Carmichael’s situation could be likened to being, say, someone who’s tone-deaf and yet wants to be a singer—he can’t learn to do this one thing that most people could, but it’s still not a super common or necessary life skill.

But, if Magery is actually very rare in the populace, then it’s more like the analogy I used before: photographic memory, a rare trait that the lack of having only really affects you if you want to go into a profession that requires it. (I don’t actually know if any professions require photographic memory, but whatevs.)

So, which one is it? How common is Magery in Sentinels? Well, let’s look at the evidence: Soothsayer C. is literally the only character we know of who has this condition; every other character who’s tried to learn magic in SC has been able to do so. There could be some sampling bias in this, of course, as we only really see the stories of exceptional people.

Of course, this is all going about things from the Watsonian perspective. The Doylist answer would probably just be “Write whatever story you want, as long as it makes some amount of sense.” (And that last bit ain’t even necessary.)

Another thing is that the “mutants as minorities” thing isn’t 100% logical either. E.g., Gay people can’t mind control the President or blow up a whole city.

fjur:

Another thing is that the “mutants as minorities” thing isn’t 100% logical either. E.g., Gay people can’t mind control the President or blow up a whole city.

True, but very few of the anti-mutant groups in the X-Men setting display any sort of logical concern about the powers of mutants; they seem to object to the mutants themselves, making no real distinction between continent-movers like Erik “Magneto” Lensherr and purely powerless innocents like Barnell “Beak” Bohusk. The latter are targeted because they’re easy prey, but if you’re only concerned about the danger posed by mutant powers, they shouldn’t be prey at all. In the middle of course are the primary pool of victims, such as the shapeshifter Raven “Mystique” Darkholme, those whose powers might be harmless or might be dangerous, but which by their nature cause paranoia about the harm they MIGHT cause, regardless of how unlikely it is that they actually will.

posts.name: Trajector
posts.cooked:
Robert Hooke! Read a fascinating dual biography of him and Edmund Halley called “Out of the Shadow of a Giant.” Hooke is known today almost solely for Hooke’s Law, which governs the relationship between force and displacement in springs. But he was the Royal Society’s experimentalist in residence and came up with all kinds of physics demonstrations and observations, including a good fraction of the stuff credited to Sir Isaac Newton! Hooke even realized the inverse square law of gravity and the idea that gravity is a property of mass before Newton did. In fact, Newton probably came up with his story about the apple as an obfuscation to claim credit for the idea first, and had such a fued with Hooke that, after Hooke’s death, Newton ordered the only portrait of him destroyed. Newton’s famous quote, “if I have seen further, it is because I have stood on the shoulders of giants” was actually a dig at Hooke, who was very short.

In summary, Isaac Newton was a jerk and Robert Hooke laid the real foundations of experimental physics, thank you for coming to my TED Talk.

(Halley was also fascinating…as a wealthy patron of science he bought a ship and crew, made himself captain, and sailed around doing scientific expeditions.)

QotD: Who is a historical figure who you think is obscure and underappreciated?

My answer is undoubtedly Dr. William Thornton. He was an American physician and polymath from the late 1700s and the early 1800s, and an all-around radical guy; here’s a brief overview:

  • He was a steampunk inventor, having designed a steamboat boiler, a steam-powered gun, and a steam-powered organ that would be heard throughout a whole city.
  • He grew up on a slave-worked plantation, yet he was staunchly abolitionist; he proposed a colony in Africa where freed slaves could go to escape persecution; his ideas eventually influenced the founding of the country of Liberia.
  • He won the contest to design the U.S. Capitol Building and the White House, despite having zero formal training in architecture; his designs were just that much more majestic than those of the other contestants, even those who were actual architects.
  • He was good friends with George Washington. When Washington died, Thornton wanted to attempt to bring him back from the dead using science! But for some reason no one let him try.
Quote from Thornton about Washington's death, 1819

“My feelings at that moment I cannot express! I was overwhelmed with the loss of the best friend I had on Earth . . . The weather was very cold, & [George Washington] remained in a frozen state, for several Days. I proposed to attempt his restoration, in the following manner. First to thaw him in cold water, then to lay him in blankets, & by degrees & by friction to give him warmth, and to put into activity the minute blood vessels, at the same time to open a passage to the Lungs by the Trachaea, and to inflate them with air, to produce an artificial respiration, and to transfuse blood into him from a lamb. If these means had been resorted to, & had failed all that could be done would have been done, but I was not seconded in this proposal; for it was deemed unavailing. I reasoned thus. He died by the loss of blood & the want of air. Restore these with the heat that had subsequently been deducted, and as the organization was in every respect perfect, there was no doubt in my mind that his restoration was possible.”

  • He was the first Superintendent of the U.S. Patent Office, and during the War of 1812’s Burning of Washington D.C., pretty much every building in the capitol was destroyed…except the Patent Office, because Thornton convinced the attacking soldiers not to.
Quote from R. Beresford, 1886, about Thornton's saving of the Patent Office

“A story is told of [William Thornton] that, during the war of 1812, when the British captured the city of Washington and destroyed the Capitol building, a loaded cannon was trained upon the Patent Office for the purpose of destroying it, and he is said to have put himself before the gun, and in a frenzy of excitement exclaimed: ‘Are you Englishmen or only Goths and Vandals? This is the Patent Office, a depository of the ingenuity of the American nation, in which the whole civilized world is interested. Would you destroy it? If so, fire away, and let the charge pass through my body.’ The effect is said to have been magical upon the soldiers, and to have saved the Patent Office from destruction.”

So, yeah. William Thornton was rad, and way cooler than Alexander Hamilton.
